title: Biomimetic Design for Adaptive Building Façades: A Paradigm Shift towards Environmentally Conscious Architecture
authors: Ali M. A. Faragalla and Somayeh Asadi, 2022
central_proposition: Biomimetic design methodologies, by mimicking nature's adaptive strategies, offer an efficient and sustainable paradigm shift for developing multifunctional adaptive building façades that optimize energy performance and enhance occupant comfort.

concept_definitions.name: Façade
concept_definitions.definition: The exterior or skin of a building, including any special architectural features.

concept_definitions.name: Adaptive Façades
concept_definitions.definition: Building envelopes that can adapt to changing boundary conditions, such as short-term weather fluctuations, diurnal cycles, or seasonal patterns.

concept_definitions.name: Biomimetics
concept_definitions.definition: The study of biological structures, processes, and their potential technological applications.

concept_definitions.name: Biomimetic Adaptive Building Skins (Bio-ABS)
concept_definitions.definition: A façade typology that responds to environmental conditions by changing its morphological or physiological properties or behavior constantly to meet the building's various functional requirements and improve its performance.

concept_definitions.name: Adaptability (CABS property)
concept_definitions.definition: Building envelopes with this characteristic can take advantage of the opportunity to act deliberately in response to changes in climatic conditions.

concept_definitions.name: Evolvability (CABS property)
concept_definitions.definition: The ability to keep options open preserves opportunities to respond to changes in the future.

concept_definitions.name: Multi-ability (CABS property)
concept_definitions.definition: Accomplishing multiple objectives sequentially rather than concurrently.

argument_structure: The paper establishes the critical role of building façades in energy consumption and indoor comfort, highlighting the shift towards performance-driven design. It introduces adaptive façades and positions biomimicry as a key innovative approach. It reviews existing biomimetic design methodologies and frameworks, detailing their components and underlying logic. Finally, it discusses the current state of biomimetic materials and simulation, identifies limitations in current applications, and proposes future research directions to advance the field.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The core mechanism involves translating biological adaptation strategies (physiological, morphological, and behavioral thermoregulation, multifunctionality, self-organization) from living organisms and ecosystems into architectural design solutions for building façades. This process enables façades to dynamically respond to environmental changes, thereby optimizing energy performance, enhancing occupant comfort, and promoting sustainability, much like natural skins regulate an organism's internal environment.

findings.antecedent: Building façades designed with biomimetic methodologies
findings.consequent: Efficiency in energy consumption and environmental performance
findings.mechanism: Biomimicry allows designers to extract organisms' functional and operational characteristics and natural adaptation strategies, translating them into innovative, adaptive, flexible, and more efficient design solutions for optimal energy consumption.
findings.quote: the biological paradigm is becoming more integrated into today's architectural design discourses [28].
findings.empirical_support_cited: The existence of such diverse yet related biological mechanisms can inspire innovative solutions for optimal energy consumption in buildings [15].

findings.consequent: Minimization of building energy load and CO2 emissions
findings.mechanism: Adaptive façades respond to dynamic outdoor environments by regulating natural light, solar protection, and harnessing energy, thereby reducing reliance on artificial systems and improving energy efficiency.
findings.quote: the design approach will not only ensure the production of adaptive, intelligent, or smart envelopes which serve both the occupants and the environment
findings.empirical_support_cited: potential of the adaptive façades to significantly minimize the building energy load and CO2 emissions while preserving occupants' thermal and visual comfort [3].

findings.antecedent: Building façades behaving more like natural skins (mimicking live organisms' adaptation)
findings.consequent: Increased versatility, resilience, and energy efficiency of buildings
findings.mechanism: Live organisms adapt to changing weather conditions while maintaining stable internal temperatures through physiological, morphological, and behavioral thermoregulation. Mimicking these abilities allows façades to dynamically adjust to environmental factors, requiring less energy to operate.
findings.quote: the ability of building façades to adapt to their microenvironment would increase their versatility and improve their resilience by requiring less energy to operate and allowing for much more efficient utilization [11].
findings.empirical_support_cited: the ability to live organisms to adapt to changing weather conditions while keeping their body temperature within very narrow ranges using physiological, morphological, and/or behavioral thermoregulation mechanisms [35].

findings.consequent: Multifunctional and adaptable façades across days and seasons
findings.mechanism: Bio-ABS integrates biomimetics as a design generator and adaptive building skins as the product, drawing inspiration from biological adaptation mechanisms that dynamically change physical or physiological conditions in response to environmental factors.
findings.quote: biomimetic façades rely on biomimetic strategies that are often driven by biological adaptation mechanisms in response to environmental factors.
findings.empirical_support_cited: researchers have become increasingly interested in the development of biomimetic building façades with an aim to achieve multi-regulation façades, which are multifunctional and adaptable across days and seasons [46].

findings.consequent: Innovative, sustainable, and adaptive building façades
findings.mechanism: These approaches allow designers to either identify a design problem and seek natural precedents or start with biological knowledge to develop environmentally responsive functions, systems, and solutions, moving beyond simple imitation of forms to complex strategies.
findings.quote: different complex strategies can be transformed from biology to architecture.
findings.empirical_support_cited: The biomimetic approach to design goes beyond simple inspiration or imitation of natural forms or processes [51,66-68].

findings.antecedent: Integration of biological principles (exchange with environment, order/structure/growth, adaptability)
findings.mechanism: These principles, observed in natural systems, guide the design to optimize material use, adapt to changing circumstances, increase resilience, and manage resources sustainably, leading to environmentally conscious architecture.
findings.quote: The concept of sustainability demanded that architectural design approaches be reviewed considering environmental and energy concerns [80].
findings.empirical_support_cited: These principles are abstract biological strategies that can be found in most organisms, some of which are obvious and self-explanatory. [55,69,70]

findings.antecedent: Biomimetic design focusing on multifunctional morphologies
findings.consequent: Optimized building façade performance in managing multiple environmental factors simultaneously
findings.mechanism: Nature provides examples of organisms (e.g., termite mounds, skink scales) that integrate multiple functions to manage heat, air, water, and light concurrently. Selecting such multifunctional biological inspirations allows for integrated solutions in building façades, addressing interconnected environmental factors more effectively than single-function solutions.
findings.quote: when faced with the task of developing a multifunctional system, it is best to select morphologies with multifunctional abilities where integration has already been effectively developed and utilized by the organism [81].
findings.empirical_support_cited: In nature, some organisms have multifunctional capabilities and can deal with multiple environmental aspects at the same time. [81]

findings.consequent: Aid for designers with inadequate biological knowledge in conceptual biomimetic design
findings.mechanism: The model organizes and categorizes biophysical data based on hierarchy and relational connections, creating a contextual map that helps designers identify relevant natural analogies and viable scenarios for design solutions, particularly for thermoregulation.
findings.quote: the model provides a frame for organizing and categorizing biophysical data based on hierarchy and relational connections, enabling the designer to perceive the biophysical data as a contextual map and to distinguish relevant analogies.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Badarnah [35] proposed a model for representing biophysical information to aid designers with inadequate biological knowledge in the conceptual design stage.

findings.consequent: Architects' ability to find biological solutions for building thermal characteristics and requirements
findings.mechanism: This cross-disciplinary framework systematically links design challenges (e.g., thermal performance issues) to biological thermal regulation mechanisms (passive/active strategies) found in nature, facilitating the transfer of these principles to architectural design.
findings.quote: This cross-disciplinary tool requires the identification, classification, and categorization of thermal regulation mechanisms utilized by organisms.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Imani et al. [83] developed a thermo-bio-architectural framework (ThBA)... to enable architects to find biological solutions which relate to the thermal characteristics and requirements of buildings.

findings.consequent: Achievement of multifunctionality in Bio-ABS design
findings.mechanism: This top-down approach uses biological metaphors and a phased process to match functional performance parameters to biological strategies, outlining properties of selected biological systems as hierarchical and heterogeneous structures to integrate multiple biological mechanisms for climate-adaptability.
findings.quote: This primarily means creating a multifunctional system in which multiple biological mechanisms should be chosen, whether they belong to the same biological model or not.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Kuru et al. [84] developed 'multi-Biomechanism Approach ‘framework aiming at achieving multi-functionality in Bio-ABS.

findings.antecedent: Bio-inspired materials (e.g., smart materials, surface structures, material architectures, targeted application technologies)
findings.consequent: Enhanced performance and innovation in adaptive façade design
findings.mechanism: These materials, inspired by biological systems, can alter properties in response to external factors, provide repellant/anti-reflective surfaces, enable lightweight/nano-scale structures, and improve system efficiency, contributing to more dynamic and responsive façades.
findings.quote: These materials represent the production of new materials with many potential applications in the initial stages of architectural design.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Bioinspired materials can be categorized into four: (1) smart materials that change and react in response to external factors; (2) materials with innovative surface structures and enhanced functions; (3) bio-inspired materials that focus on advanced geometries and structural configurations; and (4) technologies that improve existing systems by integrating specific adaption strategies [52,88,89].

findings.antecedent: Adaptive Manufacturing (AM) of bio-inspired building components
findings.consequent: Realization of intricate, self-assembling, and self-healing bio-inspired structures
findings.mechanism: AM employs a bottom-up approach, encoding material structure in precursors that self-assemble, allowing for the creation of complex, hierarchical structures and the integration of self-organization biological strategies like self-healing and self-cleaning.
findings.quote: The ability of AM to easily manufacture intricate structures allows for extensive research into structure-property relationships in biological materials [87].
findings.empirical_support_cited: AM employs a bottom-up approach inspired by nature. In this approach, the final structure of the material is encoded in precursors that self-assemble to the prescribed form. [87]

findings.antecedent: Combining dynamic Building Performance Simulation (BPS) tools with evolutionary optimization algorithms (e.g., MOO)
findings.consequent: Accurate prediction and optimization of biomimetic adaptive façade performance
findings.mechanism: Bio-ABS properties change over time, making conventional simulation difficult. This combined approach allows for visualizing trade-offs between conflicting design objectives and identifying optimal solutions (Pareto front), overcoming the complexity of digital modeling and simulation.
findings.quote: the use of multi-objective optimization (MOO) algorithms is especially useful in supporting high-performance building design because it allows for the visualization of trade-offs between two or more conflicting design objectives [43].
findings.empirical_support_cited: Clayton et al. [43] suggested a theoretical framework to overcome by combining dynamic building performance simulation (BPS) tools with evolutionary optimization algorithms, which has proven to be a valuable approach.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: The performance of biomimetic adaptive façades can be quantitatively assessed and optimized using combined dynamic building performance simulation and multi-objective evolutionary algorithms.
Buildings incorporating biomimetic adaptive façades will demonstrate significantly lower energy consumption and CO2 emissions compared to conventional buildings in varying climatic conditions.

The integration of multifunctional biomimetic morphologies in building façades will lead to superior simultaneous management of heat, air, water, and light compared to single-function façade solutions.
Designers utilizing the Biophysical Information Representation model will demonstrate increased efficiency and accuracy in identifying relevant biological analogies for specific design problems.
The application of bio-inspired materials and adaptive manufacturing techniques will result in building components with enhanced self-assembly, self-healing, and dynamic response capabilities.
bridge_warrants: The paper explicitly connects biomimicry to environmental sustainability, energy efficiency, and occupant comfort (thermal, visual, acoustic).
It links biological adaptation mechanisms to building performance, drawing parallels between natural skins and building envelopes.
It highlights the interdisciplinary nature of biomimetic design, requiring collaboration between biologists and architects.
methodological_critiques: Existing biomimetic design frameworks are still at a conceptual level and not widely tested [82].
The focus of existing methodologies on a limited type of species restricts the potential biological strategies adopted into buildings [86].
Most studies on biomimetic adaptive façades are conceptual and lack quantitative performance analysis [81].
Most buildings already built using biomimetic methods have failed to fully retain the traits of the imitated organism or biosystem [34].
Translating theoretical adaptation concepts into functional building envelopes that interact with their surroundings remains a challenge [65].
The complexity of transforming biological strategies into architectural strategies requires multidisciplinary approaches, including input from biologists and architects.
Extensive research is required to validate biomimetic strategies, their applications in the building sector, and their corresponding scales [65].
The advancement of biomimicry in engineering and technology is restricted to specific scales for transferring biological strategies from nature to design [52].
Research in biomimetic thermal solutions for buildings lacks a systematic representation of thermal interactions and their primary contribution to a system [35].
Conventional façade performance descriptors do not typically change properties over time, making Bio-ABS performance prediction difficult due to their time-varying properties [93].
Simulation tools are a crucial factor limiting the prediction of biomimetic adaptive façades' performance due to the complexity of digital modeling and simulation processes [88].
The Abdel-Rahman [93] model remains theoretical and only addresses the façade's thermal aspects.
The design and construction of buildings with adaptive façades tend to cross multiple engineering fields, necessitating a high level of coordination among involved professionals [98].
Conducting a life-cycle assessment (LCA) is a significant barrier to effectively realizing adaptive façade prototypes [99].
There is a difficulty in evaluating adaptive building façade performance due to a lack of comprehensive performance evaluation criteria, testing, assessment, and monitoring [100].
The limitation of existing simulation software and methods hinders biomimetic application in adaptive façade design [35].
Building performance is frequently not assessed, which can be viewed as a shortcoming [22].
model_structure: The paper presents three conceptual frameworks: 1) The Biophysical Information Representation Model (Badarnah [35]), a hierarchical model connecting 'Designer' and 'Biologist' through 'Challenge,' 'Processes,' 'Factors,' 'Functions,' 'System,' and 'Pinnacles' to arrive at a 'Solution' (Figure 3). 2) The Thermo-Bio-Architectural Framework (ThBA) (Imani et al. [83]), a cross-disciplinary tool with two sides (biology and architecture) linked by analogy, identifying, classifying, and categorizing thermal regulation mechanisms (passive/active) to inform architectural design parameters. 3) The Multi-Biomechanism Approach (Kuru et al. [84]), a four-phase, top-down framework: a) Identify design problems/functional requirements, b) Investigate biological solutions/match parameters, c) Achieve multifunctionality via hierarchical/heterogeneous biological structures, and d) Develop biomimetic strategies/adaptive façade configurations (Figure 4).
limitations: Biomimicry has been used in building design to a limited extent to date.
Conceptual effectiveness of biomimetic transfers does not always work in practice due to organismal design constraints and dimensional realms.
It is rare to develop holistic architectural solutions that fully adapt to the potential of biological principles.
The main challenge is addressing the monofunctionality of systems when multiple contradictory and complex functional aspects need to be addressed simultaneously.
The translation of theoretical adaptation concepts into functional building envelopes that interact with their surroundings remains a challenge.
The focus of existing methodologies on a limited type of species restricts the potential biological strategies adopted into buildings.
Multifunctionality is not fully integrated into biomimetic façades and requires further development.
A limited number of biomimetic buildings have been realized or prototyped, with most studies remaining conceptual and lacking quantitative performance analysis.
Buildings using biomimetic methods have often failed to fully retain the traits of the imitated organism or biosystem.
The inherent operational and organizational structures of engineering companies or architectural firms hinder the successful integration of bio-inspired design processes.
The advancement of biomimicry in engineering and technology is restricted to specific scales for transferring biological strategies from nature to design.
Standard and universal parameters for scaling biological systems are still lacking.
The design and construction of adaptive façades necessitate a high level of coordination among multiple engineering fields.
Conducting a life-cycle assessment (LCA) is a significant barrier to effectively realizing adaptive façade prototypes.
There is difficulty in evaluating adaptive building façade performance due to a lack of comprehensive performance evaluation criteria and monitoring.
Existing simulation software and methods have limitations in predicting the performance of biomimetic adaptive façades.

paper_metadata.crossref_title: Biomimetic Design for Adaptive Building Façades: A Paradigm Shift towards Environmentally Conscious Architecture
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: A change in thinking has been ongoing in the architecture and building industry in response to growing concern over the role of the building industry in the excessive consumption of energy and its devastating effects on the natural environment. This shift changed the thinking of architects, engineers, and designers in the initial phases of a building’s design, with a change from the importance of geometry and form to assessing a building’s performance, from structure to a building’s skin, and from abstract aesthetics to bio-climatic aesthetics. In this context, sustainable, intelligent, and adaptive building façades were extensively researched and developed. Consequently, several typologies, strategies, and conceptual design frameworks for adaptive façades were developed with the aim of performing certain functions. This study focuses on the biomimetic methodologies developed to design adaptive façades because of their efficiency compared to other typologies. A comprehensive literature review is performed to review the design approaches toward those façades at the early stage of design. Then, the theoretical bases for three biomimetic frameworks are presented to gain an overall understanding of the concepts, opportunities, and limitations.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Applying biomimetic principles to building façades can lead to adaptive, environmentally conscious architecture, improving energy efficiency and environmental performance by mimicking natural systems' strategies for adaptation and resource optimization.

mechanism_chain.description: Biomimetic design principles enable building façades to dynamically adapt to environmental conditions, leading to optimized indoor climate regulation, reduced energy demand, and improved environmental performance.
